Openlayer is a Software Development company. Openlayer is an AI governance and observability platform for regulated enterprises that allows users to test, monitor, and govern every model, agent, and AI system their company runs. Openlayer employs 32 people (+39.1% YoY, +9 people) and has an annual revenue of $1M, founded in 2021. Headquartered in San Francisco, California, United States.   > “When a governance program cannot say how many AI systems are in production, who owns each one, or how they compare in severity, that is a methodology failure.”
  >
  > Our very own Nicholas Baker (Head of Governance at Openlayer) opens his new paper with a problem enterprise AI teams are running into as their AI footprint grows: governance needs a way to identify, qualify, and quantify risk consistently.
  >
  > The three problems are distinct:
  >
  > → Identification: Do you know what AI systems are running and who owns them?
  > → Qualification: Can you consistently describe the risk each system carries?
  > → Quantification: Can you compare those risks and decide where to focus?
  >
  > The paper also explores how nuclear power and aviation moved from qualitative risk assessment toward probabilistic models as incident data accumulated, and what AI governance can learn from that transition.

  > Huge week for AI, from cheaper frontier models to new questions around how autonomous systems operate in the real world. Here’s everything we were watching over the past week:
  >
  > 1. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, the same underlying model with different safeguard levels. Fable is available for general enterprise use, while Mythos is restricted to trusted access programs focused on cybersecurity and life sciences.
  >
  > 2. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Sol and Luna, with API prices dropping significantly. Sol starts at $2 per million input tokens, while Luna starts at $0.10, bringing the cost of running AI systems down further for developers building agents and AI applications.
  >
  > 3. AI governance moved further into the international conversation, with the UN Security Council holding discussions around AI and international security. Frontier labs are also working toward more consistent approaches to evaluation and auditing.
  >
  > 4. An OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to an Australian government portal. The agent was retrieving information from a Medicare statistics service and went beyond its intended access, reaching public and non-public files. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed the incident publicly, with a forensic investigation underway.
  >
